title: Cognitive Biases
description: Name the way the mind goes wrong, and why it feels right at the time.

cards.front: Looking for evidence that fits what you already believe, and not for evidence against it
cards.note: The fix is not "try harder to be fair" — it is to go looking for the disconfirming case on purpose.

cards.front: Judging a decision by how it turned out rather than by what was known when it was made
cards.hint: A good bet can still lose
cards.note: Poker players call the loose version of this "resulting".

cards.front: The first number you hear pulls every later estimate towards it
cards.note: It works even when the anchor is obviously arbitrary, which is why opening offers matter.

cards.front: Judging how likely something is by how easily an example comes to mind
cards.note: Vivid, recent and frightening events are recalled easily, so they feel more common than they are.

cards.front: Sticking with something because of what you have already spent on it
cards.note: The money is gone either way; only the future costs and benefits should count.

cards.front: Believing, after the fact, that you knew it all along
cards.note: It quietly destroys the record of what was actually uncertain, so no lesson gets learned.

cards.front: Someone good at one thing is assumed to be good at unrelated things
Only studying the things that made it through, and drawing conclusions from them
cards.note: Abraham Wald's answer: armour the places the returning bombers were *not* hit.

cards.front: Assuming other people share your knowledge, tastes or beliefs more than they do
Explaining someone else's behaviour by their character and your own by your circumstances
cards.note: They are late because they are careless; you are late because the traffic was bad.

cards.front: Being far more confident in your judgement than your accuracy justifies
cards.note: Asking for a range you are 90% sure of, then checking how often it contained the answer, is the standard calibration test.

cards.front: Preferring to avoid a loss more strongly than to make an equal gain
cards.note: Roughly two to one in most experiments, which is why framing something as a loss changes behaviour.

cards.front: Knowing something so well that you cannot imagine not knowing it
cards.note: It is the reason experts write bad instructions.

cards.front: Preferring the current state simply because it is the current state
Rating a whole experience by its peak and its ending rather than its average
cards.note: Kahneman's colonoscopy studies: a longer procedure with a gentler ending was remembered as better.

cards.front: Continuing to believe a claim after the evidence for it has been retracted
cards.note: A correction works better if it replaces the story rather than just denying it.

cards.front: Treating money differently depending on which pot you have put it in
cards.note: A £50 refund is spent more freely than £50 of salary, though the money is identical.

cards.front: The least skilled are the least able to see that they are unskilled
cards.note: The same lack of knowledge that causes the mistakes also hides them.

cards.front: Reading meaning into random noise — a face in the clouds, a trend in a coin toss
Wanting something more because it is scarce, or because it was hard to get
Judging a group by the most extreme members you happened to notice
cards.hint: Forgetting how common the thing actually is
cards.note: The classic case: a test that is 99% accurate for a disease one person in ten thousand has still gives mostly false positives.

cards.front: Deciding what is true by what most people around you seem to think
